notable.what: The Pāli alone says the mind's states are “made of mind” (manomayā). Patna, Gāndhārī, Sanskrit and Tibetan all say “swift as mind” (manojavā).
notable.why: The most quoted line of the Dhammapada is, on this evidence, the outlier. “Made of mind” invites the reading that mind constructs experience; “swift as mind” stresses the speed with which mind leads. The teaching that mind comes first stands in every tradition either way.

notable.what: Enmity is ended “by non-enmity” in the Pāli and Patna, “by not resenting” in the Chinese, but “by patience” (kṣānti) in the Sanskrit and Tibetan.
notable.why: A negation (simply not returning enmity) against a named virtue to cultivate (patience). For practice, one says what to stop; the other what to develop.

notable.what: What overthrows the undisciplined person is Māra in the Pāli and Patna, but passion (rāga) in the Gāndhārī, Sanskrit and Tibetan.
notable.why: A personified tempter against a plain mental state. The same verse can read as mythic or psychological depending on the tradition.

notable.what: Where the Pāli praises faith and energy, the Sanskrit speaks of wakefulness and the Tibetan of mindfulness; the Chinese and Tibetan drop faith.
notable.why: The list of qualities that protect a practitioner shifts from faith toward attentiveness in the northern texts.

notable.what: The worthy wearer of the robe has self-control and truth (Pāli, Patna) or self-control and gentleness (Gāndhārī, Sanskrit, Tibetan).
notable.why: Two different virtues define the true renunciant: truthfulness, or gentleness of manner.

notable.what: The remembered injury includes a blow (“he struck me”) in the Pāli and Patna; in the Sanskrit, Tibetan and the related Chinese it is all words (“they spoke against me”).
notable.why: The teaching on letting go of grudges applies either way; the Pāli makes the injury physical, the northern texts verbal.

notable.what: Only the Gāndhārī says the mind is “unguarded / well guarded”; every other tradition says “undeveloped / well developed”.
notable.why: Guarding (a protective practice) against developing (a cultivating one). A lone reading, so it does not change the Blend, but it shows a different emphasis.

notable.what: The Tibetan ends verse 1 with “like a head cut off by a wheel”; its own Sanskrit source and every other tradition have the wheel following the ox's foot.
notable.why: A translation event inside the Tibetan, not an older reading. A reminder that a translation can carry its own errors or reinterpretations.

notable.what: The Chinese recasts several lines in moral terms: “clever words, many wants”, “that is self-made calamity / self-made blessing”, a herd of cattle instead of a cowherd counting others' cows.
notable.why: The 3rd-century Chinese translator reads the verses as plain ethical advice in his own idiom. It shows how one early reader understood them.

notable.what: The Pāli's portrait of the practitioner who lives the teaching (letting go of passion, hatred and delusion; fully aware; mind released; clinging to nothing) has no counterpart in the Gāndhārī or Udānavarga, whose versions are shorter.
notable.why: The fuller description of liberation may be an expansion in the Pāli (Patna shares only part of it), or a loss elsewhere. The Blend keeps it (R-T3-04).

patterns.statement: Where the Pāli has a negation or a general quality, the Udānavarga (Sanskrit and Tibetan) tends to name a specific virtue or practice to cultivate: patience, wakefulness, mindfulness.
Pāli and Patna keep mythic or concrete images (Māra; a blow) where the Gāndhārī and Udānavarga have psychological or verbal ones (passion; words).
The Pāli can be the outlier, even in its best-known lines; agreement among the others is a real check on it.
The Chinese is better read as an early interpretation than as a separate wording of the verse: it moralizes and uses its own images.
Many Tibetan departures are translation events (reordering, formulaic lines, misreadings), not older readings.
